title: Supporting a sow in labour
subtitle: Reading the signs and knowing when to step in.
excerpt: A sow's labour has a clear shape, and most of it needs nothing from you. Knowing which signs indicate a straightforward farrow and which mean a problem is the job. Here is what to watch for from the first signs of nesting through the final piglet.
sourceNotes: DEFRA Code of Practice for the Welfare of Pigs (2003), sections on farrowing and neonatal care. AHDB Pork, Farrowing Management manual (2018). Bill Lambkin and the Pig Veterinary Society, Practical Pig Husbandry for Small-Scale Producers (2nd edn., 2019). Alison Doggett, The Pig in the Orchard (2017).

glossaryTerms.definition: The process of a sow giving birth to a litter of piglets.
The first milk a sow produces after farrowing, rich in antibodies. Piglets must receive it within 12 hours of birth.

content.text: A sow about to
farrow

will tell you she's close. Most litters arrive without intervention. Your job is to be present, stay quiet, and know the difference between a sow working normally and one that needs a hand. The labour itself takes 2 to 6 hours from first piglet to last.
Signs farrowing is within 24 hours
The sow starts rooting and carrying bedding material into a heap. Outdoor sows dig energetically. This nesting behaviour usually begins 12 to 24 hours before the first piglet.
The vulva enlarges and reddens. Check morning and evening from day 112 of gestation onwards; gestation is 114 to 115 days on average.
Milk can be expressed from the teats 24 to 48 hours before farrowing. A thin stream when you squeeze a teat gently is a reliable pre-labour indicator.
The sow becomes restless, standing and lying repeatedly. This phase can go on for an hour or more before the first piglet arrives.
Setting up before she farrows

A warm, dry, draught-free farrowing area is the most important preparation. In cold weather, position the heat lamp 50 cm above the bedding in one corner to create a warm zone where piglets can move away from the sow. Fresh dry straw bedding gives the sow purchase and keeps newborns off cold ground.
Have clean warm towels or a dry sack ready. Piglets born weak or chilled need drying immediately. Keep them in the
creep area
under the lamp between feeds.
During labour: what normal looks like
The sow will lie on her side and begin pushing. The first piglet often takes 15 to 45 minutes after active labour begins. Subsequent piglets arrive every 10 to 25 minutes.
Each piglet may arrive in a membrane sac. Clear the sac from the face if the sow doesn't do this herself, then rub the piglet dry.
Let the piglet find a teat on its own. The suckling instinct activates quickly. Early access to
colostrum
within the first 30 minutes is critical for immunity.

Once all piglets are born, the sow passes the afterbirth (placenta). This is normal. Remove it before she eats it if possible; consumption causes no harm but makes it harder to check that all placentas have passed.
When to intervene
Active straining for more than 45 minutes with no piglet delivered. This is a stuck pig: call your vet.
Bright red bloody discharge before any piglets, or more than a cup of blood during labour, is abnormal.
A gap of more than 60 minutes between piglets with the sow still straining. Manual assistance or veterinary intervention is needed.
Green or black fluid before the first piglet may indicate placental separation; call the vet promptly.

If you need to feel inside the sow for a stuck piglet, wash your arm thoroughly, use plenty of lubricant, and work slowly in a resting phase between contractions. Manipulate the piglet into the birth canal rather than pulling hard.
After the last piglet
Count the piglets against the number of teats. A sow has 12 to 16 teats. Litters larger than her teat count will need supplementary feeding or fostering onto another sow.
Check each piglet is suckling within the first hour. A piglet that stands off to one side and shakes is chilled. Dry it, warm it under the lamp, and return it to the sow.
Offer the sow water as soon as farrowing is complete. She will be thirsty and needs to maintain milk production.
Record the date of farrowing, number of live births, number of stillbirths, and total litter weight in your holding record. UK legislation requires you to keep these records for three years.

attrs.cue: Piglet is breathing but too weak to suckle
attrs.cause: Chilled, or the runt of a large litter with low birth weight
attrs.fix: Dry and warm the piglet. Tube-feed 5 ml of colostrum if it still will not suckle after 30 minutes in the warm. Repeat every 2 hours.

attrs.cue: Sow is aggressive toward her piglets after farrowing
attrs.cause: First-litter sow (gilt) inexperience, or the sow has been disturbed and is stressed
attrs.fix: Remove the piglets temporarily to a warm box under the lamp. Allow the sow to settle. Reintroduce one at a time at a rear teat, holding the sow still.

attrs.cause: Incomplete expulsion; can cause uterine infection
attrs.fix: Call the vet. A retained placenta in a sow needs veterinary treatment.
